body_markdown:
A project car is often even more of a blank slate than you realize. While it’s easy to picture the cosmetic changes and even some of the performance upgrades, most of us fail to fully grasp what we are changing, and why, and whether said change will have the desired effect. Gauging the results of your work is especially tough when you’ve built a machine that you know can easily eclipse the flow of traffic and catapult itself and you into license-revocation territory.[My LS-swap Corvette](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/project-corvette/) is the first time I’ve had a vehicle with such capability, and thus, it’s also the first car I’ve owned that I took to the racetrack. That trip was great—and also terrible.


Last winter, the 1985 Corvette that[began as an impulse purchase](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/i-bought-a-corvette-without-really-trying/) spiraled into an overpowered grand tourer that took me almost all summer to sort out. Even after solving many of the small problems that pop up in an involved project such as this, and finally[re-gearing the Dana 44 differential](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/my-ls-swapped-corvette-returns-to-jackstands/) from a 3.07:1 to 4.10:1 ratio, the car is still in need of work. However, it has reached a level of functionality that allows me to get the first real feel for what this car is—and more importantly, what it could be. As regular readers will know, this car is not even remotely “done” in the way that most project cars are.


Even incomplete, this car has a lot of capability—far more than is safe to use or get acclimated to on the street, especially in a Northern Michigan tourist town whose back roads will soon be inundated with color tours. Evaluating whether the 400 horsepower I put under the hood will actually hook up when the skinny pedal hits the floor is not something to be done in traffic. So I talked to a couple of friends and discovered that they were hosting a track day at[Grattan Raceway](https://grattanracewaypark-mx.com/) in Belding, Michigan, on a weekend I was available.


After renting a trailer, loading up a bunch of tools, and doing one final nut-and-bolt check, I headed for the track to see whether this Corvette was going to leave me wanting more—or if maybe, just maybe, this project came out right the first time.


The trusty red Express van served valiantly as tow pig.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The Express also served as home for a few days, because I am too cheap to pay for a hotel near the track.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Morning dew was the only moisture, which was welcome after the last time I was at Grattan in the rain.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Grattan is a super fun track, as I found out[the last time I went](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorcycles/even-in-the-rain-the-track-is-safer-than-the-street/) , on two wheels. While most tracks that feature elevation changes were carefully crafted by some designer, Grattan feels like someone let a 9-year-old drive the paving machine around their parents’ backyard—including all the parts that are better suited for sledding (e.g., the uphill, off-camber, 50-mph left turn). Grattan keeps a driver busy yet has a nice long front straight to allow you to take a quick relaxing breath and check the gauges before diving back in.


In a well-prepared car, this track is quick and engaging. On a motorcycle, this track is downright fun. Behind the wheel of an overpowered 41-year-old Corvette that still sports its original-equipment (OE) Bilstein shocks and suspension bushings? Well, it’s *very* interesting. Or, at least, that’s what I expected. Like the first time taking anything I’ve owned or built to the track, I did only a handful of laps during the first session, at an ever-increasing but still very conservative pace, to give the things I might have forgotten a chance to show themselves prior to pushing any braking or turn-in point. Five laps in, I extended my hand out the window as I approached turn four to signal to anyone behind me that I was exiting the track for the pits.


Back in the paddock, the news was all good. No fluids had escaped their containment vessels. No new clunks, vibrations, or noises had popped up. It was almost like I knew what I was doing. In the days before loading the car onto the trailer, I took an afternoon to replace the brake pads, soft lines, and fluids with items appropriate for track usage, so cutting the first session short to double-check everything early was just a cheap bit of insurance. During the next few sessions, I picked up the pace a bit more, pushing the throttle a little earlier and harder, starting to get a feel for how the car wanted to be driven.


Trailer parking first thing in the morning is always a fun sight.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


A quick drivers’ meeting started the day just like so many other track days.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Cars in attendance varied wildly, but everyone was well behaved.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The third session felt as though both the car and I were starting to really get a handle for each other. Before long, I was stalking the bumper of a red[Scion FR-S](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/the-original-scion-fr-s-subaru-brz-is-the-millennial-generations-datsun-240z/) that was running clean lines and pulling me into a nice groove. Sure, I could have easily won every drag race down the front straight, or casually pushed the throttle a little more on the back straight to leave that FR-S in my rearview mirror, but he would have been filling my mirrors before we had even tracked out of turn one. I was having a fun time trying to hang with a much more modern, significantly more appropriate-for-Grattan machine through the corners. So much so that I committed one of the cardinal sins when tracking junky stuff.


I forgot to keep track of the gauges.


Whether because I was looking out for pointing by faster drivers or simply because I was wrestling with an overpowered yet tired-out Corvette, I simply forgot to take a long look at the gauges displayed on a phone screen mounted to the center of the dash. The information came directly from the Holley engine control unit, and by the time I did remember to glance down, the coolant temperature had spiked above 220 degrees, and the brake pedal was beginning to soften from multiple entries into turn one at 120 mph. In what was likely a mild panic, I dove off the track into the pits, knowing there was a non-zero chance that, if the radiator overflowed, it could put that coolant right on the passenger front tire. (Not something I want to experience.)


With the hood up to bleed off heat and a fan tucked under the bumper to flow more air across the radiator, I took a deep breath and gathered myself to take stock of the situation. Turns out, the iron-block V-8 survived the heat just fine. Some coolant was pushing out of the overflow tank, but that didn’t happen until the car was stationary in the pits. Sometimes, it takes both preparation and luck to get home safely. I quickly realized that pulling the car onto the trailer was the only thing left to do: The power steering pulley looked a little off, and upon further inspection, I found that the pump was loose, and the bolts holding the pump to the cast aluminum bracket that also holds the alternator came out with the aluminum threads still attached. Three short sessions in, and the day was done.


Racetracks and puddles do not go together.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


When the tools come out, it’s rarely a good sign.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Oh, are those threads important?


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Before anyone runs to the comments to say “bummer” or talk of how unfortunate this is, know that this outcome was not only expected but welcome. As with any such situation at a racetrack, there was much talk in the paddock about field repairs and what would be necessary to get the Corvette back out on track. I shrugged off all of it. Identifying weaknesses is exactly what testing is for, and the Corvette will come back stronger, safer, and even more fun. How? We’ll get into that in the next update, but just know that winter is right around the corner, and that means I’ll be spending a lot of time snowed into my garage. That’s plenty of time to bring the chassis up to the level of the powertrain—or maybe not. Stay tuned!
